quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of probabilistic modeling over deterministic machine learning?
options: Probabilistic models run in O(1) time complexity on GPUs
Probabilistic models estimate the entire predictive distribution P(y|x), quantifying prediction uncertainty and confidence intervals rather than only outputting a single point estimate
Deterministic models cannot process numerical features
Probabilistic models guarantee 100% classification accuracy on unseen data
quiz.explanation: Deterministic models produce single fixed values (e.g. house price = $750k) with no indication of confidence. Probabilistic models estimate P(y|x) (e.g., mean $750k with 90% predictive interval [$680k, $820k]), which is critical for risk assessment in healthcare, autonomous driving, and finance.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between generative and discriminative probabilistic models?
options: Generative models only work on text, while discriminative models only work on tabular data
Generative models learn the joint distribution P(X, Y) = P(X|Y)P(Y) modeling how data was produced, whereas discriminative models directly model the conditional distribution P(Y|X)
Discriminative models always require prior distributions
Generative models cannot perform classification
quiz.explanation: Generative models (e.g., Naive Bayes, Gaussian Mixture Models, VAEs) model the joint probability P(X, Y) and can generate synthetic samples. Discriminative models (e.g., Logistic Regression, probabilistic neural networks) focus solely on predicting the target conditional distribution P(Y|X).

quiz.question: In Bayesian inference P(θ|D) = [P(D|θ) P(θ)] / P(D), what does each component represent?
options: θ is learning rate, D is depth, P(θ) is momentum
P(θ) is the prior belief; P(D|θ) is the likelihood of observed data given parameters; P(θ|D) is the updated posterior distribution; and P(D) is the marginal likelihood (evidence)
P(θ|D) is the training error; P(D|θ) is the validation loss
P(D) is always zero in continuous distributions
quiz.explanation: Bayesian inference formally updates prior parameter beliefs P(θ) upon observing dataset D by multiplying by the data likelihood P(D|θ) and normalizing by the evidence P(D) = ∫ P(D|θ)P(θ) dθ to obtain the updated posterior P(θ|D).

quiz.question: What defines a conjugate prior in Bayesian statistics?
options: A prior distribution that has a mean of zero and variance of one
A prior distribution that, when multiplied by the likelihood, yields a posterior distribution belonging to the exact same algebraic probability family as the prior
A prior that can only be evaluated using Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) sampling
A prior that completely ignores observed training data
quiz.explanation: When the prior and posterior belong to the same distribution family (e.g., Beta prior + Binomial likelihood = Beta posterior; Normal prior + Normal likelihood with known variance = Normal posterior), the prior is conjugate. This enables exact closed-form analytical updates without numerical integration.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation?
options: MLE maximizes the likelihood P(D|θ) alone, while MAP maximizes the posterior P(θ|D) ∝ P(D|θ)P(θ) by incorporating a prior distribution over parameters
MLE produces a full probability distribution, while MAP produces a single number
MAP is only valid for discrete classification
MLE incorporates prior domain knowledge, whereas MAP does not
quiz.explanation: MLE finds θ_hat = argmax P(D|θ), relying solely on observed training frequencies and being vulnerable to overfitting on small datasets. MAP finds θ_hat = argmax P(D|θ)P(θ), incorporating prior domain constraints that pull parameter estimates toward plausible baselines.

quiz.question: How is L2 regularization (Ridge) mathematically interpreted through Bayesian MAP estimation?
options: As MAP estimation under a Uniform prior distribution on weights
As MAP estimation under an independent zero-mean Gaussian prior distribution w ~ N(0, τ²I) on the model weights
As MAP estimation under a Laplace prior distribution
As maximizing the marginal likelihood with infinite variance
quiz.explanation: Taking the negative logarithm of the posterior with a Gaussian prior w ~ N(0, τ²I) yields -log P(w|D) = Negative Log-Likelihood + (1 / 2τ²) ||w||₂². The Gaussian prior directly penalizes large squared weights, establishing that L2 regularization is equivalent to Gaussian MAP estimation.

quiz.question: In Bayesian Decision Theory, why should a decision system minimize expected loss rather than simply picking the outcome with highest predicted probability?
options: Because probabilities cannot be computed in real-time systems
Because the real-world operational costs of different mistakes (e.g. False Negative vs False Positive) are asymmetric; a low-probability event with catastrophic cost may demand immediate action
Because expected loss always equals zero in optimal classifiers
Because Bayesian decision theory only applies when probabilities are exactly 50%
quiz.explanation: In medical screening, missing an aggressive disease (False Negative, cost = 1,000) is far worse than conducting a follow-up biopsy on a healthy patient (False Positive, cost = 10). Even if P(Disease) is only 8%, the expected loss of doing nothing far exceeds the cost of intervention.

quiz.question: What is a Gaussian Process (GP) in probabilistic machine learning?
options: A deep neural network with Gaussian activation functions
A non-parametric Bayesian approach that defines a prior probability distribution over continuous functions, specified by a mean function m(x) and covariance kernel k(x, x')
An algorithm for sorting numerical arrays in O(N log N) time
A clustering method identical to K-Means
quiz.explanation: A Gaussian Process f(x) ~ GP(m(x), k(x, x')) generalizes multivariate Gaussian distributions to infinite-dimensional function spaces. Any finite collection of input points has a joint Gaussian distribution, producing exact analytic predictive distributions with grounded uncertainty bounds.

quiz.question: What is the critical distinction between aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty?
options: Aleatoric uncertainty is measured in decibels, while epistemic is measured in percentages

Aleatoric uncertainty represents inherent stochastic randomness or observation noise in the data (irreducible), whereas epistemic uncertainty represents lack of model knowledge in sparse data regions (reducible by gathering more training data)
Epistemic uncertainty cannot be evaluated using probability
Aleatoric uncertainty only occurs in deep neural networks
quiz.explanation: Aleatoric uncertainty is irreducible observation noise (e.g. sensor thermal noise, unpredictable human behavior). Epistemic uncertainty reflects the model's ignorance due to limited training data (e.g., predicting outside historical feature ranges); it shrinks toward zero as more representative data is collected.

quiz.question: Why is high classification accuracy insufficient to verify whether a probabilistic model is well-calibrated, and what does the Brier Score or Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measure?
options: Accuracy only measures discrete label match; a model can be 90% accurate while severely overconfident (predicting 99.9% probability when true confidence is 60%), which ECE and Brier score detect by measuring probability calibration
Accuracy is undefined for binary classification
ECE can only be computed when dataset size N < 100
Brier Score only measures computational training latency
quiz.explanation: A model predicting 0.99 confidence for every correct prediction and 0.99 confidence for its errors will have high accuracy but disastrous overconfidence. Calibration metrics (reliability diagrams, ECE, Brier score) measure whether events predicted with probability p actually occur with frequency p across repeated trials.
